chunks.title: Ocular symptoms: what to ask
chunks.tldr: Three symptom families: vision, appearance, pain/discomfort. Characterise onset, duration, frequency, laterality, severity, triggers, treatments tried. Ask about diabetes, hypertension, steroids, allergies, family history (glaucoma, strabismus, RD, AMD). Clues: myopic blur worse in dim light (big pupil); central cataract worse in bright light; corneal oedema blur better as the day goes on.
points: Transient loss: vascular (amaurosis fugax) or migraine scotoma.
Flashes: instantaneous = retinal traction; seconds–minutes = migraine.
Monocular diplopia (persists with other eye covered) = optics: refractive, cataract, cornea.
Binocular diplopia: incomitant (varies with gaze) = palsy/restriction; comitant = long-standing squint.
Surface pain relieved by anaesthetic drop; deep ache = glaucoma, iritis, endophthalmitis, scleritis.
Itch = allergy; chronic epiphora = drainage problem; lids glued shut = infective conjunctivitis.
chunks.hook: Anaesthetic fixes surface pain, not deep pain.

cards.q: Blurred vision from corneal oedema typically changes how through the day?
cards.a: It improves as the day progresses (evaporative dehydration of the cornea).

chunks.title: Visual acuity, pinhole & poor vision
chunks.tldr: Distance acuity at 20 ft (6 m), near at 14 in (33 cm); always each eye separately. Snellen fraction = test distance / letter size row (20/60 = reads at 20 ft what normal reads at 60). Tumbling/illiterate E from ~3½ years. Pinhole blocks misfocused rays → if acuity improves, the problem is refractive. Can't read 20/200: move closer (5/200) → CF → HM → LP → NLP.
points: Corrected acuity reflects ocular health; uncorrected may just be refractive error.
Refraction both prescribes and diagnoses (refractive vs other blur).
Binocular acuity matters for function, e.g. driving.
chunks.hook: Pinhole helps → it's the glasses, not the eye.

cards.q: What does improvement with pinhole indicate?
cards.a: The reduced acuity is due to refractive error.

chunks.title: Confrontation fields, pupils & RAPD
chunks.tldr: Confrontation: patient and examiner close opposite eyes, compare fields with finger counting in 4 quadrants; red target for subtle desaturation. Visual neglect (right parietal): sees each side alone but misses the left with simultaneous stimuli. Pupils: size, shape, light + near; dim room shows a small pupil, bright room a large one. Swinging light test: affected pupil dilates when light swings to it = RAPD — optic nerve (or extensive retinal) disease; not caused by cataract, corneal opacity or vitreous haemorrhage.
points: RAPD can be read from one pupil only — useful if the other pupil is damaged/unseen.
Pupil abnormalities: neurological, inflammation (spasm/synechiae), high IOP (atony), surgery, drugs, normal variants.

cards.q: Does a dense cataract cause an RAPD?
cards.a: No — media opacities do not cause a relative afferent pupillary defect.

chunks.title: Motility, external & slit lamp
chunks.tldr: Corneal light reflex: reflex temporal = esotropia; nasal = exotropia (works in infants). Cover test: cover one eye, watch the other for a refixation movement; prism cover test quantifies. Versions in cardinal gazes: palsy, myasthenia, restriction (e.g. floor fracture). External: lid position, palpebral fissure, proptosis, rim palpation, preauricular nodes, temporal artery. Slit lamp 10–16×, stereoscopic; optical section localises depth; shows cells/flare.
points: Lid eversion (patient looks down, applicator at upper tarsal border ~8–9 mm above lashes) whenever a foreign body is suspected.
Fluorescein + cobalt blue: punctate staining (dryness, UV) to big defects (abrasion, ulcer).
chunks.hook: Reflex goes temporal when the eye turns in.

cards.q: Corneal light reflex displaced nasally in one eye indicates?

chunks.title: Special lenses & tonometry
chunks.tldr: Gonioscopy needs a mirror lens (Goldmann, Posner–Zeiss) or direct Koeppe. Goldmann 3-mirror: angle + mid/far periphery + central. Volk (90D/78D) non-contact posterior pole view. Normal IOP 10–21 mm Hg. Goldmann applanation: force to flatten cornea; endpoint = fluorescein mires' inner edges touch. Thin cornea → true IOP higher than measured; thick → lower (pachymetry). Pascal dynamic contour ignores thickness. Portable: Perkins, Tono-Pen; Schiøtz (old); air-puff (screening, less accurate).
points: Don't press on the globe while measuring.
Disinfect contact tonometer tips.

cards.q: Effect of a thick cornea on Goldmann IOP?
cards.a: Overestimates — true IOP is lower than measured.

chunks.title: Diagnostic drops
chunks.tldr: Anaesthetics: proparacaine, tetracaine, benoxinate. Dilation: phenylephrine 2.5% (α-agonist, dilator) + tropicamide 0.5–1% (anticholinergic, also cycloplegic) — combination fastest (15–20 min) and widest. Measure IOP before dilating (small rise); check for narrow angles (oblique penlight) — risk of acute angle closure. Avoid excess drops (nasopharyngeal absorption).

cards.a: Dilation can raise IOP slightly and may precipitate angle closure.

chunks.title: Direct vs indirect ophthalmoscopy
chunks.tldr: Direct: monocular, 15×, ~10° field, portable. Red reflex at arm's length: moving opacity = vitreous; fixed = lens/cornea. Your right eye for their right eye; get close. Cup:disc ratio; disc 1.5–2 mm (1 DD); fovea ~2 DD temporal to disc. Indirect (BIO): binocular/stereo, ~3.5× with 20D, ~37° field, bright light (sees through haze), reaches ora serrata with scleral depression; image inverted. Used for RD assessment and surgery.
points: Red-free filter: vessels and nerve fibre layer.
Small spot for undilated pupils.
Non-ophthalmologists: check acuity in children, refer diabetics for dilated exams, refer suspicious discs — amblyopia, DR, glaucoma are the big preventable blinders.

cards.q: Three advantages of indirect over direct ophthalmoscopy?
cards.a: Brighter light through hazy media, stereoscopic view, view of the entire retina to the ora with scleral depression.

chunks.title: Perimetry & Amsler grid
chunks.tldr: Fields measured in degrees; sensitivity highest at fixation. Static: stimulus at fixed spot, brightness increased to threshold (automated Humphrey). Kinetic: fixed target moved inward → isopters (Goldmann, tangent screen). Automated printout: threshold dB (higher = better), total/pattern deviation, MD, PSD, reliability (fixation losses, false +/−). Amsler grid: central 20° × 20° (each square 1°) at reading distance; scotoma or metamorphopsia (macular fluid) — home monitoring in AMD.
points: Needs steady fixation, fixed distance, standard background and targets, standard protocol.
Pattern deviation removes generalised loss (e.g. cataract).
chunks.hook: Wavy lines on Amsler = fluid under the macula.

cards.a: Static: thresholds at fixed locations (automated). Kinetic: moving fixed target maps isopters (Goldmann).

chunks.title: Colour, contrast, glare, potential & functional loss
chunks.tldr: Congenital red–green deficiency: X-linked, ~8% of males, <0.05% females; blue–yellow (tritan) <1%, not sex-linked. Acquired: optic neuritis/compression → red–green (before acuity drops); glaucoma & macular disease → blue–yellow. Plates: Ishihara (red–green), HRR (both), City University. Contrast sensitivity drops with cataract/retina/nerve disease despite 20/20. Glare (brightness acuity) for cataract/corneal oedema. Potential acuity meter projects chart through clear media gaps (imperfect). Functional loss: tunnel field that doesn't expand at 2 m; same lines read at every distance.
points: Exclude advanced glaucoma, RP, cortical blindness before calling it functional.

cards.q: Prevalence of congenital red–green colour deficiency in males?
Tangent screen sign of functional visual loss?
cards.a: Field doesn't double in diameter when testing distance doubles from 1 m to 2 m (tunnel field).

chunks.title: Microbiology, cornea, tears & orbit tests
chunks.tldr: Conjunctival scraping: Giemsa (cell types), Gram (bacteria). Corneal ulcer: scrape → plate directly (no transport medium); any growth significant. Endophthalmitis: aqueous tap (25G parallel to iris) or better vitreous; PCR for viral retinitis. Keratometry (2 meridians; astigmatism, IOL calc), topography, wavefront (higher-order aberrations), specular microscopy, pachymetry. Schirmer: <5 mm in 5 min with anaesthetic = abnormal. Rose bengal stains devitalised cells. Jones I (dye recovered from nose?) → Jones II (irrigation). Hertel: normal 12–20 mm, eyes within 2 mm.
points: Jones II: dye recovered after irrigation = partial obstruction; clear fluid = pump failure; no flow = total occlusion.
Exophthalmos = increased orbital content (haemorrhage, tumour, inflammation, oedema).

cards.q: Normal Hertel measurement and acceptable asymmetry?
cards.a: 12–20 mm, with ≤2 mm difference between eyes.

chunks.title: Fundus photos, FA, ICGA, OCT & FAF
chunks.tldr: Stereo disc photos: track glaucomatous cupping. Fluorescein: blue excitation, green emission; normal vessels don't leak; RPE masks choroidal flush; macula darker. Leakage (late cloud) = permeability; non-perfusion; haemorrhage blocks. ICGA: big, protein-bound, sees through RPE/blood/exudate → occult CNV, choroid. OCT: 840 nm light echo, ~5 µm resolution, non-contact, undilated OK — macular oedema, RNFL/disc (glaucoma, often before field loss); OCT-A without dye; anterior segment OCT 1300 nm. FAF: lipofuscin map.
points: Ultrasound resolution ~100 µm vs OCT ~5 µm.

cards.q: Why is ICGA better than fluorescein for imaging the choroid?
cards.a: ICG is fully protein-bound (stays in choroidal vessels) and its infrared fluorescence passes through RPE, blood and exudate.

chunks.title: Ultrasound, CT/MRI & electrophysiology
chunks.tldr: A-scan: 1-D spikes — axial length for IOL power, tumour size. B-scan: 2-D image through opaque media (RD, tumour: solid/cystic/calcified). Doppler: flow reversal in carotid occlusion or CCF. CT: bone, orbit, foreign body, calcium (retinoblastoma). MRI: intracranial/optic nerve disease; contraindicated with metallic FB. Flash ERG: whole-retina (RP, dystrophies, siderosis) — not focal/macular or ganglion disease. Pattern ERG: P50 macula, N95 ganglion cells. EOG: Arden ratio; Best disease = abnormal EOG, normal ERG. VER: whole pathway; demyelination prolongs latency; objective acuity in infants/malingerers. Dark adaptation: rod disease.
